newsitem.title: RUSSIA: U.S. PLD Telekom sees Russia future with Rostelekom.
newsitem.headline: U.S. PLD Telekom sees Russia future with Rostelekom.

text.p: A U.S. long-distance telephone company plans to expand its Russian domestic operations through cooperation with local telecoms powerhouse Rostelekom, the only way to work in Russia, industry analysts said on Friday.
U.S.-based PLD Telekom expects cooperation with Russia's international and national long-distance carrier Rostelekom to increase in the coming year.

"In 1996, of our total group revenues, probably less than 20 percent was associated with Teleport," a domestic long-distance joint venture approximately equally owned by Rostelekom and PLD, said Simon Edwards, chief financial officer for PLD.
"We see that venture as the one which has the most potential for growth going forward, and we'll see that percentage rapidly rising in 1997 and 1998."

PLD, which mainly uses satellite technology, is about one-third owned by Britain's Cable & Wireless. It also has holdings in companies operating international long distance gateways from Russia and Kazakhstan.
Industry sources said PLD and US West's Russian Telecommunications Development Corporation unit (RTDC), which operates Russian cellular phone networks, are also talking about a merger.
Both companies declined to comment on a merger, although Edwards said PLD was interested in acquiring and expanding its business.

London's Financial Times newspaper said a merged company would challenge Rostelekom and Svyazinvest, the state-owned national telecoms holding company which Russian officials have said will be given a controlling stake in Rostelekom.

But Western telecoms analysts said that Rostelekom, with strong infrastructure for international and domestic long distance built over the past few years and strong political contacts, would be unlikely to allow strong competition.
"Whatever happens, Rostel is going to be the dominant one," Ruth Belbin, telecoms analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell said.

"Now that the basic infrastrucure have been built, we see Rostelekom positioning itself more strategically rather than granting limited operating rights which it was certainly doing in the early days when the infrastructure was not there."
Russia granted Western providers international long distance licences for that market, which grew rapidly after the break-up of the Soviet Union in 1991.

But Rostelekom has set up a long-distance network largely without the help of foreign partners, despite years of negotiations with RTDC, in a consortium with France Telecom and Deutsche Telekom, which produced no real result.
"Ros has done a fairly good job of setting up its own networks without the help of its supposed strategic partners," said Alfa Capital telecoms analyst Kristen Burton Steiner.

"I would strongly doubt that any licences independent of participation with Rostelekom would be granted... but the size of anything PLD comes up with in terms of Teleport is going to be dwarfed by Rostelekom's present infrastructure."

One Western analyst said PLD, with its growing satellite infrastructure, which the company says will expand to include joint ventures in more than 45 cities this year from under 20 currently, could make a good fit with RTDC's cellular customers.
"RTDC has customers across Russia, and PLD is a long-distance provider. One's got customers and the other one has networks," the analyst said.
But operating independently of Russia's telecom behemoth would be a bad idea, the analyst said. "You would have to be out of your mind to challenge Rostelekom and Svyazinvest."
